analysis:
Examined the two changed files. In SelfUpdater.swift the only change is line 65: `now` goes from private to internal (module-visible). It is a Sendable closure that only supplies a timestamp. It grants no signing-bypass or install capability. The production init (lines 81-90) still hard-codes verifyCodeSignatures: true. Stage and commit paths (lines 407-629) are unchanged: tree hash recheck, code signature verification, and runtime capability verification. Internal visibility is weaker encapsulation, but I see no security regression.

In UpdateRecoveryState.swift, `rollbackSource` is added (base lines ~305). `completeRollback` now also works when there is no pending candidate: it takes `current` when `current != predecessor.release`, sets current to the predecessor, and quarantines the replaced version with failureCount 0. This only changes local state, and the quarantine is single-slot and scoped to the exact version. The quarantine/anti-downgrade posture of T-043 is preserved, because isNewer still blocks reinstalling the quarantined version unless manualOverride is set. A promoted release can now be rolled back by watchdog logic, which I could not see in the supplied units (WatchdogRecoveryService and the callers of completeRollback). The open question for integration is whether the callers physically restore the predecessor files before completeRollback records current = predecessor. If state were written without the filesystem restore, the recorded installed version would be inconsistent with the disk. That would only affect update-comparison logic and could not install an unverified binary. Rollback restoration code (UpdateRecoveryStore) was not supplied, so I cannot confirm it. Relevant threat: T-043 (watchdog rollback authority). I identified no concrete finding. A deeper review of the unchanged callers is advisable.
